catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beda-mayr:
Beda Mayr was a Bavarian Benedictine philosopher, apologist, and poet, born near Augsburg in 1742, who died in 1794. He took vows at Heiligenkreuz in 1762, was ordained in 1766, and taught mathematics, philosophy, rhetoric, theology, and canon law there. An exemplary religious and popular preacher, he absorbed Kant's subjectivistic criticism as a philosopher and was irenic beyond measure as a theologian.

In a letter to Henry Braun, he argued that Catholic-Protestant unification was possible, and Braun published it without consent in 1778. Augsburg's bishop censured him and temporarily barred him from teaching theology. His chief work, defending natural, Christian, and Catholic religion in three parts (1787-90), was placed on the Index in 1792. Lindner counts fifty-eight productions, including twenty-one dramas and four sermon volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confession-bu:
F. M. Rudge's entry traces confession, from Latin confessio, first a martyr's burial place, also called memoria or martyrion. Use widened over time to the altar over the grave, the underground chamber holding the tomb, and the high altar over the confession. Later it meant the basilica itself, and finally a new resting place after transfer. On transfer, relics went to a crypt below the high altar, or a hollow beneath it, behind a pierced screen, as in the catacombs.

The tomb stayed open, touched by the faithful with brandea cloths, later venerated as relics. At Saint Clemente the urn of Clement and Ignatius shows behind such a screen. Confession lamp oil counted as relic. Rome's famed underground confessions include San Martino ai Monti, San Lorenzo with Laurence and Stephen, and Santa Prassede with Praxedes. Greatest stands Saint Peter's, where Anacletus raised a memoria and Constantine built the Confession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-neumayr: A 1913 entry on Franz Neumayr — the Jesuit preacher. Edward Garesché honors his famous sermons. His voice shook the Munich pulpits. The order prized its eloquent son. The Bossuet of the German Jesuits. His 1765 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johannes-thur: This 1913 reference article on Thurmayr — the Bavarian annalist. Patricius Schlager honors his famous Annales. His pen chronicled the German past. The dukes prized the weighty tomes. The scholars mine his pages. His 1534 death is famed. His 1534 Annales are famed. His 1534 German annals are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyr: This 1913 reference article on the Martyr — the blood-witness. Maurice Hassett unfolds the sacred lore. He seals the faith with death. The Church keeps the holy names. The calendar marks their feasts. Its 1907 study is famed. Its crowning death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edmund-the: St. Edmund the Martyr was the king of East Anglia. This long entry examines his crown, his Danes, and his cult. The saint of the Bury shrine: his martyr's arrows sealed Hoxne in the 869 of the Danes in the east.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edward-the: St. Edward the Martyr was the boy king of England. This entry traces his Corfe, his murder, and his cult. The saint of the Wareham shrine: his martyr's blood sealed Corfe in the 978 of the plot in the castle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-justin-mar: St. Justin Martyr was the philosopher apologist. This very long entry examines his Apologies, his Rome, and his crown. The martyr of the second century: his martyr's blood sealed Rome in the 165 of the empire in the city of the Caesars.
the-vale-of-cedars-or-the-martyr:
Grace Aguilar's The Vale of Cedars, or The Martyr, appeared in 1851 with a memoir of the author placed before the story. Aguilar was born at Hackney on June 2, 1816, eldest child of Emanuel Aguilar. Her family descended from Jews of Spain who fled persecution and found asylum in England.

The memoir stresses a contrast between frail health and an early, eager mind. Sickly from infancy, she spent summers by the sea under doctors' care, yet learned to read almost without trouble and asked always for books as presents. Her mother was nearly her only teacher. She kept a journal from age seven and, before twelve, had begun writing, already observant on family tours of English cathedrals and manufactories.
